newsitem.title: UK: Labour resolute against guerrilla violence -Blair.
newsitem.headline: Labour resolute against guerrilla violence -Blair.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair told the IRA on Monday that voters would not be cowed by its disruption of Britain's election campaign and he vowed that if elected prime minister he would never bow to guerrilla violence.
"The IRA's attempts to disrupt the election campaign in Britain will not succeed," he wrote in the Irish Times newspaper.
"The British people will not be moved by terrorism. Nor will a new Labour government. We will be firm and resolute in the face of violence."
The run-up to Thursday's election has been clouded by a wave of Irish Republican Army bombs and hoax warnings that have paralysed parts of the transport system on the British mainland.
On Sunday the IRA, which wants a place for its Sinn Fein political wing in Anglo-Irish sponsored multi-party talks, admitted planting a bomb which exploded near an English motorway last Friday.

Blair, tipped by opinion polls to unseat John Major's Conservatives, said he would not change a bi-partisan policy to the peace process that insists the IRA must declare a truce for Sinn Fein to get a place in talks, due to restart on June 3.
"We will look to both (Protestant and Catholic) traditions in Northern Ireland to seek out the common ground between them and to build a new and peaceful future upon it," the Labour leader said.
Anglo-Irish talks adjourned in deadlock in March to allow local politicians prepare for Thursday's election.

Sinn Fein, which says it hopes to win three seats at the election, has been excluded from talks because the IRA refuses to call off a war it has waged for 28 years against British rule in the province.
"There must be a genuine ceasefire from the IRA. It must be proven to be genuine in both word and deed," Blair wrote.
Labour was committed to promoting reconciliation between the province's majority Protestants, who support rule from London, and the minority Catholics who want to be ruled from Dublin.

Blair signalled to Protestant hardliners that Labour would not tolerate a repeat of last summer's choas that erupted during a period of annual pro-British parades, some of which went through Catholic areas.

Labour would do all it could to facilitate local agreement about controversial parades, he pledged. "Labour is determined -- this and every year -- that the rule of law will be upheld," he wrote in the Dublin-based paper.
